questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is admitted with a three-day history of vomiting and reduced oral intake. Creatinine has risen from a baseline of 82 to 198 µmol/L (60-110). Urine output over the last 8 hours is 0.4 mL/kg/hr.
questions.lead: What KDIGO stage of acute kidney injury does his creatinine indicate?
options: Cannot be staged without a urine output over 12 hours
questions.explanation: Creatinine has risen to 2.4× baseline (82 → 198), which falls in the 2.0-2.9× band = Stage 2. Stage 1 is 1.5-1.9× or a rise of ≥26.5 µmol/L; Stage 3 needs ≥3.0×, creatinine ≥353.6, or starting RRT. His urine output of <0.5 mL/kg/hr for 8 hours meets Stage 1 by that criterion — and when creatinine and urine criteria disagree, the higher stage applies.
questions.point: KDIGO Stage 2 AKI is a creatinine rise of 2.0-2.9 times baseline, and when criteria disagree the higher stage applies.

questions.stem: The same patient's urinary sodium is 14 mmol/L and urine osmolality 640 mOsm/kg. There is no hydronephrosis on ultrasound.
questions.lead: What is the most likely cause of his AKI?
questions.explanation: Low urinary sodium (<20) with concentrated urine (>500 mOsm/kg) means the tubules are intact and appropriately conserving salt and water — the kidney is responding correctly to hypovolaemia, so this is pre-renal. In established ATN the tubules have failed: urinary sodium rises above 40 and the urine becomes inappropriately dilute. Normal imaging excludes obstruction.
questions.point: Pre-renal AKI shows urinary sodium under 20 with concentrated urine; ATN shows urinary sodium over 40 with dilute urine.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy develops dark urine two days into a sore throat. BP is 112/70, urinalysis shows blood 3+ and protein 1+, and complement C3 is normal.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Haematuria appearing during the infection — synpharyngitic, within 1-2 days — with a normal C3 is IgA nephropathy. Post-streptococcal GN occurs 1-2 weeks after the infection, with a low C3 that normalises by 6-8 weeks, and usually hypertension and oedema. Timing and complement together decide it; either alone is insufficient.
questions.point: IgA nephropathy causes haematuria during infection with normal C3; post-streptococcal GN follows 1-2 weeks later with low C3.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old presents with periorbital oedema and frothy urine. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is markedly elevated, serum albumin is 18 g/L (35-50), and cholesterol is raised. Blood pressure is normal and there is no haematuria.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.explanation: This is nephrotic syndrome in a child — heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia. Minimal change disease accounts for the large majority in this age group and responds to corticosteroids, so treatment is started empirically and biopsy is reserved for atypical features: age under 1 or over 12, hypertension, haematuria, renal impairment, low complement, or steroid resistance. None of those are present.
questions.point: Childhood nephrotic syndrome is treated with empirical corticosteroids, with biopsy reserved for atypical features or steroid resistance.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on ramipril and spironolactone is admitted with diarrhoea. Potassium is 7.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2). The ECG shows peaked T waves with a broadening QRS.
questions.lead: What is the first drug to administer?
questions.explanation: Calcium gluconate first. It does not lower potassium at all, but stabilises the cardiac membrane within minutes and reduces the risk of fatal arrhythmia. Insulin-dextrose and salbutamol then shift potassium intracellularly, and resonium or dialysis remove it. The sequence is protect the heart, shift, remove. Also stop the ACE inhibitor and spironolactone, both of which are contributing.
questions.point: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, calcium gluconate is given first to stabilise the myocardium.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with heart failure is admitted with confusion. Sodium is 118 mmol/L (135-145). She is clinically hypervolaemic with peripheral oedema and raised JVP.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate management of her hyponatraemia?
options: Fluid restriction and treatment of the heart failure
Rapid correction with hypertonic saline to normal
questions.explanation: Hypervolaemic hyponatraemia — total body sodium is high but water is higher still. Treatment is fluid restriction plus treating the underlying cause, here the heart failure, with a loop diuretic. Giving saline adds to the overload. Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms such as seizures or coma, given cautiously, and correction must not exceed roughly 8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours because of the risk of osmotic demyelination.
questions.point: Hypervolaemic hyponatraemia is treated with fluid restriction and treatment of the underlying cause, not saline.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 44 mL/min/1.73m² and a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 38 mg/mmol (normal <3.5) on two occasions. His blood pressure is 148/86.
questions.lead: Which combination gives the greatest protection against progression of his kidney disease?
options: Dual ACE inhibitor and ARB blockade
questions.explanation: An ACE inhibitor or ARB at maximum tolerated dose reduces intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, and an SGLT2 inhibitor slows progression and reduces cardiovascular events independently of glycaemic control — together they are the current standard in albuminuric diabetic kidney disease. Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB is harmful, increasing hyperkalaemia and AKI without benefit. Expect a small eGFR dip on starting the SGLT2 inhibitor; it is haemodynamic and not a reason to stop.
questions.point: Albuminuric diabetic kidney disease is treated with an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus an SGLT2 inhibitor; dual ACE inhibitor and ARB blockade is harmful.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has recurrent renal colic. She has bilateral flank masses on examination, hypertension, and a family history of kidney disease in her father and brother. Ultrasound shows multiple bilateral renal cysts.
questions.lead: Which extrarenal complication most warrants specific consideration?
questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease — bilateral cysts, hypertension, flank masses, dominant family history. The association to know is intracranial berry aneurysm, with screening considered where there is a family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage. Also expect hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse, and diverticular disease. Sensorineural hearing loss belongs to Alport syndrome, which is the distractor here.
questions.point: ADPKD is associated with intracranial berry aneurysms; sensorineural hearing loss belongs to Alport syndrome.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 21 mL/min/1.73m²) has a haemoglobin of 89 g/L. Ferritin is 220 µg/L, transferrin saturation 26%, B12 and folate normal, and there is no evidence of bleeding.
questions.lead: What is the appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Anaemia of chronic kidney disease, from reduced renal erythropoietin production — typically appearing once eGFR falls below about 30. Iron stores here are adequate for CKD targets (ferritin >100 and transferrin saturation >20%), so this is not iron deficiency and iron alone will not help. Treatment is an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, given only once iron sufficiency is confirmed, since an ESA cannot work without substrate.
questions.point: Anaemia of chronic kidney disease is due to erythropoietin deficiency and treated with an ESA once iron stores are confirmed adequate.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man on haemodialysis has missed his last two sessions. He is breathless, with a pericardial rub, and potassium is 6.8 mmol/L with a pH of 7.18. Chest examination reveals crackles to the mid-zones.
questions.lead: What is the indication for urgent dialysis in this presentation?
options: Refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload and uraemic pericarditis together
questions.explanation: The indications for urgent renal replacement therapy are remembered as AEIOU: Acidosis (refractory), Electrolytes (refractory hyperkalaemia), Intoxication (dialysable toxins), Overload (refractory pulmonary oedema), Uraemia (pericarditis or encephalopathy). This patient meets four of the five. A pericardial rub in a dialysis patient is uraemic pericarditis and is itself a dialysis indication — it also risks tamponade.
questions.point: Urgent dialysis indications are acidosis, electrolytes, intoxication, overload and uraemia, remembered as AEIOU.
